lead: Both readings are about the word that is handed on and the fruit it bears. Paul tells Timothy to avoid quarrels about words and to be “a worker who has no need to be ashamed, rightly explaining the word of truth.” In John, Jesus reminds the disciples that they did not choose him; he chose them and appointed them to bear fruit that will last, and the fruit he names is love for one another. On the day the Panchangam remembers Mar Irenaeus, the readings fit a bishop who spent his life explaining the word of truth rightly. The key words are truth and fruit.

r.h: Rightly explaining the word of truth
set: 2 Timothy is written as Paul's last letter, from prison in Rome, to his beloved co-worker Timothy, who was leading the church at Ephesus. Many scholars think that the Pastoral Letters were written by a disciple in Paul's name after his death; others hold that they come from Paul himself near the end of his life. The Church receives them as inspired Scripture either way.

Just before our verses comes the hymn: “If we have died with him, we will also live with him” (2:11). Timothy must remind the community of this saving faith, and protect it from teachers who were spreading empty speculation; verses 17–18 name two of them, who claimed that the resurrection had already taken place.
str: v. 14: remind them; warn them not to wrangle over words.
v. 15: be an approved worker who rightly handles the word of truth.
v. 16: avoid profane chatter, which leads into impiety.
kw: Literally “to fight with words”. Not careful thought about the faith, which the Church has always needed, but quarrels for the sake of winning, which leave the listeners confused and divided.
a worker who has no need to be ashamed
The image of a labourer whose work can bear inspection. Timothy's ministry is honest work done before God, not a performance before people.
Literally “cutting straight”, like a road cut in a straight line or a furrow ploughed true. The minister of the word keeps to the straight path of the truth and leads others along it.
vv: warn them before God that they are to avoid wrangling over words, which does no good but only ruins those who are listening.
The test of any argument about faith is what it does to the listeners. Quarrels that leave people bitter or lost are not the work of the Spirit.
Do your best to present yourself to God as one approved by him, a worker who has no need to be ashamed, rightly explaining the word of truth.
This verse has become a motto for preachers and catechists. The first audience of every preacher is God.
Avoid profane chatter, for it will lead people into more and more impiety,

The same warning appears at the close of 1 Timothy: “Avoid the profane chatter and contradictions of what is falsely called knowledge” (1 Timothy 6:20). Empty talk does not stay empty; it pulls people away from God.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that the task of authentically interpreting the word of God has been entrusted to the living teaching office of the Church, which is not above the word of God but serves it, teaching only what has been handed on (Dei Verbum 10; CCC 86). St Irenaeus, remembered today, did exactly what this reading asks. Against teachers who claimed a secret knowledge, he pointed to the faith publicly handed down from the apostles through the bishops of the churches, above all the church of Rome, with which, he wrote, every church must agree (Against Heresies 3.3; CCC 834).

r.h: You did not choose me but I chose you
set: These verses belong to the Last Supper discourse. Jesus has spoken of himself as the true vine and of the disciples as branches (15:1–8), and has told them: “No one has greater love than this, to lay down one's life for one's friends” (15:13). He no longer calls them servants but friends (15:15). Now he tells them where their calling comes from and what it is for.
str: v. 16a: the initiative is his: I chose you.
v. 16b: you are appointed to go and bear lasting fruit; the Father will give what you ask in my name.
v. 17: the purpose of the commands: love one another.
kw: In the ancient world a disciple chose his teacher. Here the Teacher chooses. Every vocation begins in the unearned love of Christ, not in our own merit or plan.
Literally “I placed” or “I set”. The same verb is used when the good shepherd “lays down” his life (10:11). The one who lays down his life for his friends also sets them in their mission.
The verb menein, to abide or remain, runs through the whole chapter. Fruit that lasts grows only on branches that abide in the vine (15:5).
vv: You did not choose me but I chose you.
A word of humility and of comfort. Humility, because no one can boast of his calling; comfort, because the one who chose us knew our weakness and still chose us.
And I appointed you to go and bear fruit, fruit that will last,
The disciples are not chosen to stay in the upper room but to go. The fruit is both the holiness of their lives and the people brought to Christ through them.
I am giving you these commands so that you may love one another.
All the commands come down to one. The fruit that lasts is love.
ch: The Church hears in these words the source of every vocation, especially the call of the apostles and of their successors the bishops. The Catechism teaches that Christ chose the Twelve and made them sharers in his mission (CCC 858), and that the new commandment of love sums up the whole law of the Gospel (CCC 1970). St Augustine, preaching on this passage, says that the Lord did not choose the disciples because they were good, but made them good by choosing them (Tractates on John 86, in substance).

qa: Paul says to avoid wrangling over words. Does that mean that exact words in matters of faith are unimportant?

No. The Church has always cared about the right words: the Creed, the definitions of the councils, the words of the sacraments. What Paul condemns is quarrelling for its own sake, clever debate that serves pride and leaves the hearers worse off. Careful words that guard the truth are a service of love; empty arguments are not. St Irenaeus fought hard for the true faith, but always so that ordinary believers might keep it clearly and simply.
rite: The Panchangam remembers Mar Irenaeus today, the day on which the wider Church keeps the memory of St Irenaeus of Lyons. Born in Asia Minor around AD 130, he heard as a young man the preaching of St Polycarp of Smyrna, who had known the apostle John. He became bishop of Lyons in Gaul and wrote Against Heresies, the great defence of the apostolic faith against those who claimed secret knowledge. His name means “peaceful”, and he lived up to it, pleading with Pope Victor for peace among the churches in the dispute over the date of Easter. He taught that “the glory of God is man fully alive, and the life of man is the vision of God” (Against Heresies 4.20.7; CCC 294). In 2022 Pope Francis declared him a Doctor of the Church with the title “Doctor of Unity”. A Church that holds the faith of the apostles and longs for the unity of all Christians can pray today with him.
study: Paul tells Timothy to be a worker who need not be ashamed before God. In conversations about faith at home or online, do I seek to win, or to help the other person come closer to the truth?
Jesus says, “You did not choose me but I chose you.” How does knowing that Christ chose me change the way I look at my own vocation and my weaknesses?
